blocks.title: Wedding Food Through the Ages
paragraphs: Wedding meals have always done more than feed guests. The food on the table signals who the family is, what they believe, and how much they want to celebrate. Across centuries and cultures, wedding food has carried meaning far beyond taste.

items.prompt: What food do people often serve at weddings where you live?
items.answer: Answers will vary. People may mention cake, a family dish, a religious food, or a large meal for many guests.

items.prompt: Why might a family choose a traditional dish for a wedding?
items.answer: A traditional dish can connect the wedding to family history, culture, religion, or a shared memory.

items.prompt: How can wedding food show money or social status?
items.answer: A family might serve rare ingredients, a very large cake, or an elaborate meal to make wealth and status visible.

blocks.title: Food and Status — Part 1: Ancient Rome
paragraphs: Wedding food can show social rank as well as celebration. In ancient Rome, confarreatio, which literally meant "with spelt," was a patrician form of marriage. The bride and groom shared spelt cake and bread during the ceremony. Because patricians belonged to Rome's upper class, this simple grain food carried legal, religious, and social meaning.

items.prompt: Why did shared spelt cake and bread have more than a simple food meaning in ancient Rome?
items.answer: They were part of confarreatio, a patrician marriage ceremony. The food carried legal, religious, and upper-class social meaning.
items.explanation: What simple food has a special meaning in a ceremony you know?

blocks.title: Food and Status — Part 2: Medieval Feasts
paragraphs: Records of medieval French feasts help us understand how a noble wedding banquet could make status visible. Aristocratic tables might offer peacock, heron, or swan. Imported spices such as saffron, ginger, nutmeg, cardamom, and cinnamon came from far-off places. They were rare and valuable, so serving them showed a host's wealth and trade connections. Even the seating could show rank: the most important guest sat nearest the large salt container. Wedding food was not only a meal; ingredients and presentation helped families show their place in society.

images.alt: Watercolor illustration of a medieval French noble feast with rare spices, birds, golden serving ware, and high-ranking guests at a long table.

items.prompt: Why were imported spices important at wealthy medieval European feasts?
items.answer: Imported spices such as saffron, ginger, and cinnamon came from far-off places and were rare and valuable. Serving them showed that the host had money and trade connections.
items.explanation: Can you think of a costly or rare food that people serve at celebrations today?

blocks.title: Religion and Symbolism — Part 1: A Hindu Wedding
paragraphs: Religious wedding food does not follow one universal menu. It changes by region, community, and family. At one Hindu wedding described by Smithsonian, the bride received a coconut, which the couple then gave to the groom. The coconut was a divine offering for a blessed marriage and a symbol of prosperity. A paste of cumin seeds and brown sugar represented the bitter and sweet parts of life. Rice also appeared as a symbol of sustenance and as an offering.

images.alt: Watercolor illustration of an adult Hindu bride passing a coconut to the groom, with rice and cumin-and-brown-sugar foods nearby as symbolic wedding offerings.

items.prompt: What did one food represent at the Hindu wedding described in this part?
items.answer: The coconut was a divine offering for a blessed marriage and a symbol of prosperity. The cumin-and-sugar paste represented the bitter and sweet parts of life, while rice represented sustenance and offering.
items.explanation: Which food in your culture has a symbolic meaning at a celebration?

blocks.title: Religion and Symbolism — Part 2: A Jewish Wedding
paragraphs: Jewish weddings offer another example. Blessings over wine are part of the ceremony, and the couple drinks from a cup after the seven blessings. The feast afterwards is called a seudat mitzvah, a religiously important meal with food, dancing, and singing. Guests are encouraged to help the couple rejoice. The exact dishes vary, but the shared meal has a clear purpose. In both traditions, food turns belief into something families and guests can see, taste, and take part in.

items.prompt: What gives food and drink a religious purpose at the Jewish wedding described here?
items.answer: Wine is used for blessings during the ceremony, and the seudat mitzvah is a religiously important shared feast where guests help the couple rejoice.
items.explanation: Why can taking part in a shared meal feel different from only watching a ceremony?

blocks.title: Changing Traditions — Part 1: Wedding Cake
paragraphs: The wedding cake changed over many centuries. In seventeenth-century England, a bride cake was closer to sweet bread with fruit and spices. By the eighteenth century, fruit cakes were often covered with sugar icing. Whiter icing required better, more expensive sugar, so its color became a sign of money. At Queen Victoria and Prince Albert's wedding in 1840, the cake weighed 136 kilograms, measured about 2.7 metres around, and had detailed figures on top. It made royal extravagance easy to see. Later royal cakes became taller and more complex, and smaller, cheaper versions reached more families near the end of Victoria's reign.

items.prompt: What did Queen Victoria’s 1840 wedding cake show about wealth and fashion?
items.answer: The cake was enormous, covered in costly white icing, and decorated with detailed figures. It made royal wealth easy to see. Later royal cakes became taller and more complex, while cheaper versions gradually became available to more families.
items.explanation: Why might people copy wedding fashions used by famous or royal figures?

blocks.title: Changing Traditions — Part 2: Uzbek Plov
paragraphs: Tradition does not always mean cake. In Uzbekistan, plov is a national rice-and-meat dish served at weddings, births, funerals, and holidays. Wedding plov may include extra chickpeas, raisins, and garlic. A skilled cook can prepare one huge pot for hundreds of guests. Plov shows family memory, hospitality, and community. Together, the white cake and communal plov show two paths: wedding food can display wealth, or it can make an old shared dish feel especially joyful.

images.alt: Split watercolor comparison of a formal white wedding cake and an Uzbek community warmly sharing a large dish of wedding plov.

items.prompt: What does wedding plov show besides the family’s ability to feed many guests?
items.answer: Wedding plov shows family memory, hospitality, community, and Uzbek cultural identity. A shared traditional dish can make a large celebration feel connected.
items.explanation: Would you rather share one large traditional dish or a formal wedding cake? Why?

items.prompt: Wedding food has carried meaning related to wealth, religion, family, and identity across very different cultures and centuries. Which of these forces do you think shapes wedding food most strongly today, and has that changed compared to the past?
items.answer: There is no single correct answer. A strong response might argue that family and cultural identity shape wedding food most strongly today. The historical examples show that money and religion have also mattered: rare spices displayed wealth, while coconut, rice, and wine carried religious meaning. Couples today still balance tradition with their budget, family history, and personal taste.
